(DES 1) But for the fact that both the ORRV Report and the DES bore the same signature, one would almost be forced to the conclusion that this is another instance of the bureaugracy grown so large that the left hand can no longer assist in washing the right.
We note the parade of the conclusions throughout this DES as they assume themselves: "...no area of the public lands is free from potential damage..."

(13) "...use of machines...may rut slopes..." "Use of machines...

can affect..." (14) "Indiscriminate use of IRV...can have severe...
\neffects...." "...plant communities...can suffer...." "All wildlife is affected to some degree...." (15) The doubts of March are the suppositions of May.
On the other hand the "economic boom" noted by the ORRV Report (51)
"...both in the general market and in individual sections of rural America"\nin March had diminished by May to the "minor economic effects" of
controlled ORV use. (DES 17) The flowers of March plainly died in May;
the rites of Spring were brief this year.
This confusion that is so evident in the Department's turning its back on its own study less than two months after that ten-month-long study was completed is characterized, we believe, by the current term "future shock" which, though it may be excused by the arrogation of the Congressional function to the Presidential Office, is even more evident in the Secretarial directive of implementation of May 5, 1972. The Secretarial Memorandum, incorporated into this DES, adopts a definition of off-road vehicle totally at variance with the one prescribed by the Executive Order. The Presidential Proclamation made no exemption for logging trucks or construction equipment or farm tractors. Earth, in this instance, survived May, for the Secretaria, Memorandum copts the ORRV Report definition, without, however, Executive authority for doing so.
The President commands that you regulate all off-road vehicular use; you propose to requeste only off-road recreational vehicle use. The recreational vehicle user that but note his objection to this discrimination and wonder, perhaps, where in the rabbit warrens of official Washington sits this man who thinks that a motorcycle does more ecological damage than a logging truck.
We would suggest that a resolution of this difficulty, and most of the others that the implementation of Executive Order 11644 is certain to provoke, is to be found quite imply in supplying a definition of the word "road", for we are at a total loss in trying to understand how anyone can intelligently discuss "off-road" without first locating that which one shall not be permitted to get "off".
